t: #2237 Count Positions on Street With Required Brightness
o: Each lamp covers a contiguous interval of positions; brightness at p is the number of intervals covering p. We must count positions whose brightness meets requirement[i]. In Example 1 the coverage counts are [1,3,2,2,1] versus requirements [0,2,1,4,1], so positions 0,1,2,4 qualify (4 total). Brute-force marking each lamp's range costs O(lights × range) which can be ~10^10 — too slow. A difference-array prefix sum computes all coverages in O(n + lights).
k: Interval coverage counting is the classic difference-array + prefix-sum pattern.
Clamp each lamp's interval to [0, n-1] before applying updates.
Compare the computed brightness against requirement in a final linear pass.

a.i: For each lamp covering [l, r], do diff[l] += 1 and diff[r+1] -= 1. A prefix sum of diff then gives brightness at every position in O(n). Finally count positions meeting their requirement.
s: Create diff of size n+1 filled with zeros.
For each lamp, l = max(0, pos-range), r = min(n-1, pos+range); diff[l]++, diff[r+1]--.
Prefix-sum diff to get brightness b[i] for each position.
a.t: O(n + L) — one pass over lamps and one over positions.

a.i: Instead of a fixed-size array, create +1 events at each lamp's left endpoint and -1 events at right endpoint + 1, sort them by coordinate, and sweep while tracking the active count between consecutive event points. Useful when coordinates are huge and sparse (here they are bounded, so Approach 1 is simpler).
s: Build event list [(l, +1), (r+1, -1)] per lamp and sort by coordinate.
Sweep, maintaining active lamp count on each segment.
For each street position in the current segment, compare active count with its requirement.
a.t: O(n + L log L) — sorting the 2L events dominates.

w: Always clamp ranges before updating the difference array — an unclamped r+1 can exceed n and cause out-of-bounds writes. Note requirement comparisons are '>=' (Example 1 position 4 has equality). Follow-up: report brightness for arbitrary point queries offline — the same sweep works with binary search over events.
